title: Releaf
subtitle: Small actions. A lighter footprint.
summary: An iOS app that brings reuse ideas, carbon tracking, and a sustainability community into everyday life.
intro: Sustainability becomes more approachable when the next step is concrete. I helped build Releaf around the things people already have, the habits they want to change, and a community to share those experiments with. Under the friendly surface, the app is an exercise in putting machine learning where it is useful and keeping it honest about what it knows.
facts: kinds of item recognised on the phone
sections: From information to a daily habit

Releaf brings together ways to reuse everyday materials, an estimate of the carbon a person’s day produced, and a community for sharing what worked. The aim is to give environmental information a useful place in a routine: an idea to try, an action to record, or something to show someone else. Progress is drawn as a tree that grows through eleven levels, and rewards are counted in water drops.
A classifier that lives on the phone

The app’s current code recognises waste with an EVA-02 Large vision model converted to Core ML. One image passes through three output heads at once: 30 item classes, 15 materials and 4 bins. Running on the device means a photo does not have to leave the phone to be useful, and a prediction below a set confidence is flagged rather than presented as certain. If the on-device model is unavailable, the app can fall back to the same classifier on the server.
A small graph instead of a large model

A name is not yet advice. Releaf ships a knowledge graph of 43 nodes (30 items, 8 materials and 5 destinations) joined by 118 edges, with embeddings learned by a graph attention network. Disposal guidance is a lookup along the graph’s edges; “similar items” is a cosine similarity between embeddings. Moving search onto this graph removed the app’s dependence on an external language-model service for that feature.
Carbon tracking that separates guessing from arithmetic

The carbon tracker is opt-in. Location and motion readings are summarised on the phone into 15-second windows, and only those summaries are uploaded. A calibrated classifier infers the travel mode and reports “unknown” when its confidence is low. A separate, auditable step then multiplies distance by published emission factors. The classifier was trained on a physics-based mobility simulator, so its near-perfect simulated accuracy is not a claim about real phones.
Building with a team

As a cofounder of Rematter Cooperation, I worked across the SwiftUI app, the Django backend for accounts, rewards, achievements and notifications, and the supporting AI services. We raised $2,000 in funding and earned a top-two team placement in the 2025 China High School Social Innovation Competition and Incubation Camp. Releaf reached more than 5,000 downloads.
note: Download and funding figures are reported in my résumé. Carbon estimates are informational; they are not direct measurements of environmental impact.

technical.heading: From a photo to a useful next step.
modules: One image, three questions

The EVA-02 Large classifier takes a 448 × 448 image and answers three questions from a shared representation: what the item is, what it is made of, and which bin it belongs in. Accuracy on held-out images ranged from about 90% to 94% depending on the evaluation set, with food waste and glass bottles the weakest classes. The model was exported to Core ML at 16-bit precision for the phone.
Guidance by graph lookup

A graph attention network (GATv2) learns a 64-dimensional embedding for each of the 43 nodes. The app ships the graph as plain data, so turning a prediction into guidance is a neighbour lookup and a similarity search that work offline. Similarity scores rank candidates; they are not calibrated probabilities that a reuse idea will work.
Useful under partial failure

The supporting services split the work between a gateway, vision, retrieval, a knowledge graph and a response step. The orchestrator marks a response as partial when a service is missing, and a fallback path keeps a simpler answer available. An unavailable capability is reported instead of being papered over.
technical.footnote: These details describe the app’s current code and its supporting AI repository, which reports staging readiness. They are separate from the released app’s download figures, and not every feature described here is confirmed as released.

tour: An iOS app that makes the next sustainable step concrete. Point the phone at an object and it names the item, the material and where it should go, without sending the photo anywhere.
bridge: A phone that sorts waste on its own raises the next problem: what should software do when it is not sure of the answer?
island: A phone, a tree and five places for things to go.
limits: Download, funding and competition figures come from my résumé. They are not usage or retention figures.
Carbon numbers are estimates from distance and published emission factors. They are not measurements of a person’s real footprint.
The travel-mode classifier has only been evaluated on simulated trips. Its accuracy on real devices is not yet known.
hotspots: The app
The screen is a real screenshot of Releaf’s community feed, where people share reuse ideas.
Thirty items, five destinations
An on-device classifier recognises 30 kinds of item. A small knowledge graph links each one to a material and to one of five destinations: recycle, compost, landfill, special handling or donate.
A graph the phone can search
Items, materials and destinations stored as a graph that works without a connection. The sculpture is simplified; the real graph has 43 nodes and 118 edges.
My Tree

title: Beyond the heat map
subtitle: The hottest neighborhood is only part of the story.
summary: Remote sensing and interpretable clustering to study urban heat vulnerability across Phoenix.
intro: A surface-temperature map tells us where a city is hot. It does not, by itself, tell us which neighborhoods are most vulnerable. My research brought satellite, land-cover and census information together for 369 Phoenix census tracts to examine that difference, and to ask how much a cooling program’s priorities change when the definition of “priority” does.
facts: top-decile tracts shared by both rankings
rank correlation between the two rankings
sections: A different way to ask the question

I studied 369 Phoenix census tracts. Rather than treating temperature as the whole problem, I compared two ways of choosing where to act first: a ranking by surface temperature alone, and a ranking by a score that also counts how built-up a tract is, how many people live there, and how sensitive they are to heat.
Building one picture from eleven

Surface temperature comes from Landsat 8 and 9 Collection 2 Level-2 scenes. Eleven scenes from June to August 2024 passed quality screening; cloud, shadow and saturated pixels were masked, and the per-pixel median of what remained gave a summer composite of temperature and vegetation. The 2024 National Land Cover Database supplied paved surface and tree canopy, and the American Community Survey supplied age, poverty and housing figures with their margins of error.
A score that keeps its parts visible

The priority score is the plain average of four percentile ranks: heat, built burden (paved surface and lack of vegetation), exposure (population density) and sensitivity (people over 65, children under five, and poverty). Equal weights are a value choice, not a fitted model, and the paper says so. Keeping the four parts separate means anyone can see why a tract ranks where it does.
When the rankings diverge

Across all tracts the two rankings agree fairly well, with a rank correlation of 0.749. At the top, where decisions get made, they do not: only 17 of the 37 hottest tracts are also among the 37 highest-priority tracts. Moving from one ranking to the other shifted the median tract by 42 places, and the largest moves were about 250 places in each direction.
Three kinds of neighborhood

Clustering the tracts on seven standardised features gave three readable profiles: 206 tracts with compounded heat and socioeconomic burden; 45 low-density tracts that are far from cooling centres; and 118 greener, slightly cooler tracts with the oldest residents. The grouping stayed stable when the census inputs were perturbed within their margins of error 50 times, which is the check that lets the profiles be discussed at all.
note: Paper: “Remote Sensing and Interpretable Machine Learning for Neighborhood-Level Urban Heat Vulnerability in Phoenix, Arizona.” Submitted and accepted by my supervising professor; unpublished. “Interpretable” refers to the readable cluster profiles and the transparent score.

technical.heading: One city. Three ways to read it.
modules: From radiance to a tract

Landsat thermal values are converted to kelvin with the product’s published scale and offset, masked with its pixel-quality bands, and combined as a per-pixel median over the summer. Each raster is then summarised inside tract boundaries in a common map projection. Of 373 tracts assembled, 369 passed the coverage and quality checks.
A change in the decision rule

A temperature-only ranking and the four-part priority ranking are compared at the top decile and top quintile. Overlap is reported as counts and as a Jaccard index (0.298 at the top decile), so the result is about which places a program would visit first, not about an average difference.
Profiles that survive perturbation

k-means with three clusters was chosen after comparing three to six clusters against Ward linkage. Stability was measured by re-clustering after perturbing census variables within their margins of error: the median adjusted Rand index was 0.797 for k-means against 0.580 for Ward. Both scores are spatially clustered (Moran’s I of about 0.5), so neighboring tracts are not independent samples.
technical.footnote: Surface temperature, demographic vulnerability and intervention priority answer related but different questions. The study compares those perspectives; it does not measure the effects of a completed cooling program.

tour: A satellite can tell you where a city is hot. This study asks who lives there. Rank Phoenix’s neighborhoods by heat alone, then by heat plus vulnerability, and the two lists disagree at the top.
bridge: If one map can mislead, the next question is practical: with a limited budget, where should the next measurement go?
island: A desert city, seen from orbit and from the street.
limits: Satellite surface temperature is not air temperature, night-time heat or indoor heat.
The equal weights in the priority score are a stated value choice. Different weights would move tracts.
The study does not link any ranking to health outcomes, and distance to a cooling centre is straight-line, not travel time.
hotspots: Landsat
Eleven summer-2024 scenes from Landsat 8 and 9 were combined into one surface-temperature picture of the city.
369 tracts
Each tile stands for a census tract. Heights and colours here are an illustration, not the study’s data.
Cyan posts mark the 37 hottest tiles and coral pins the 37 highest-priority ones. Only 17 tiles carry both.

Cooling centres are the kind of decision a ranking informs. Distance to them was tested as a separate scenario.

title: ZenithSync Assay Planner
subtitle: What should an experiment measure next?
organization: AI4S Open Innovation: AI for Life Science
summary: A Gaussian-process tool for choosing informative treatment and control measurements in organoid experiments.
intro: Every measurement uses part of an experiment’s budget. Given one control and the lowest and highest doses already measured, which few wells should a lab buy next to pin down a drug’s dose-response curve? I built a planner that considers what is already known, where uncertainty remains, and how a shared control affects several treatment measurements at once.
facts: paired drug contexts in the confirmation
lower error than the greedy baseline
sections: The shared-control problem

A treatment response is read against a measured control. When several responses share that reference, their errors are related: if the control reads high, every contrast reads low together. The planner keeps this dependence instead of treating the control as perfectly known, and it can choose to buy another control well when that helps more than another treatment well.
A curve that starts at zero

The response is modelled as a Gaussian process over log dose, with a kernel adjusted so that the drug effect at zero dose is exactly zero. A control therefore carries no drug effect but still carries information, through the shared noise. Hyperparameters were chosen once by leave-one-organoid-out validation on a development dataset, where all 28 folds picked the same setting, and then frozen.
Choosing a batch exactly

For a fixed budget, the planner searches every possible set of wells and keeps the one that leaves the least average uncertainty across the planned doses. Wells that are interchangeable are grouped, so one representative stands for many equivalent sets: 13,408 representatives covered 2,113,536 subsets in the confirmation. A small counter-example in the tests shows why this matters: the best single well is not always part of the best pair.
Testing the claim on data it had not seen

The protocol was frozen and timestamped before the confirmation dataset’s responses were opened. That dataset has two parallel plates per context: wells are chosen from one and judged against the other. Across 6,496 contexts from 148 organoid samples and 100 patients, exact selection lowered mean squared error by 32.82% against random selection under the same model. Against the stronger greedy baseline the improvement was 0.66%, which is the honest size of the advantage of exact search.
What stayed in the record

On the development dataset the same comparison was inconclusive: every bootstrap interval included zero. An earlier liver-chip pilot gave no positive result either. Both remain in the repository beside the confirmation, along with a crashed first evaluator run that was preserved and amended for serialisation only.
note: These are retrospective research results. Prospective laboratory savings, clinical benefit, and transfer to perfused organ-on-a-chip experiments have not been demonstrated. Development data: Farin et al.; confirmation data: Kryeziu et al.; both public.

technical.heading: The control well is part of the model.
modules: Keep the covariance

Subtracting the same measured control from several treatment readings introduces shared error. With independent raw errors of variance s², the contrast-noise covariance is R = s²(I + 11ᵀ): 2s² on the diagonal and s² off it. The joint Gaussian model preserves that dependence; its error was 11.36% lower than an ablation that ignores it.
Search the finite design space

The optimizer chooses a fixed-budget batch by minimising the equally weighted posterior variance at the designed doses, C − C[:,A] C[A,A]⁻¹ C[A,:]. Verified exchangeable wells are grouped so one representative per count pattern is evaluated. This reduces enumeration without changing the optimum of the bounded problem, and it is checked against brute force in the tests.
Freeze, then evaluate

Model choices were fixed before confirmation on a separate public organoid study. Exact, greedy and random policies share the same prediction model and measurement budget. Inference resamples whole patients after averaging contexts within samples and samples within patients, so repeated contexts are not counted as independent evidence.
technical.footnote: The covariance objective depends on the design and observed-well locations, not the response values. This is a fixed-model batch design; predictions update with measurements, but the selection rule is not response-adaptive. The endpoint is the error of the raw log treatment-minus-control signal, not viability.
source: Read the mathematical and contribution audit

tour: Each well in a drug-response experiment costs the same, and there are never enough. This planner chooses the next few so that the response curve becomes as certain as possible.
bridge: Freeze the rules, keep the strongest baseline, then look at the result. The last island turns that habit into machinery.
island: Two plates, one curve, and three wells worth buying.
limits: These are retrospective results on public data. Savings in a real laboratory have not been demonstrated.
The nominal 90% intervals covered 98.05% of held-back readings, so they are conservative rather than well calibrated.
No clinical benefit, peer review or competition placement is claimed. I was the only team member and the only reviewer.
hotspots: Three wells to buy
With a budget of three, the demo plan picks one more control well and two treatment doses.
One control, many readings
Every treatment reading is compared with the same control, so their errors are linked. The model keeps that link.
Where the curve is unsure
The band is wide where nothing has been measured. The planner buys the wells that narrow it most.
A plate held back
Wells are chosen from one plate and judged against a parallel plate the planner never saw.

title: CollegeAdvisor
subtitle: An answer should come with a source.
summary: A college-advising application built around retrieval, citations, and knowing when information is insufficient.
intro: Admissions, financial aid, and transfer pathways all depend on specific information. At Athena AI Labs, I worked on an application that retrieves supporting material before constructing an answer, with checks for questions the available sources cannot support. The design goal was modest and strict: an answer should either show where it came from or decline.
sections: Connecting the whole application

I developed a SwiftUI interface, a Python API, and retrieval-augmented generation workflows for college-advising questions. Student-profile integration supported personalized recommendations, while document ingestion organized the information the system could consult.
Five collections, kept apart

The knowledge base is organised as five collections: financial-aid policies, major admission requirements, Common Data Set figures, transfer articulation agreements, and worked answers with their citations. Keeping them separate lets a question about transfer credit search different material from a question about aid, and lets a result say which kind of source it came from.
Retrieval before generation

A question is first matched against those collections by meaning, and results from official .edu and .gov sources are weighted above other material. The published design documents also describe keyword retrieval; the path I describe here is the dense one. The language model’s job is to phrase the answer. The retrieved evidence supplies the facts.
Cite, calculate, or abstain

Some questions should not be answered from text at all. Aid and cost figures are computed by a deterministic calculator rather than generated. Questions that ask for legal judgement, predictions or personal preference are caught before retrieval. And when the best evidence is weak, the system abstains and explains why. On the project’s own stress set, most cases were resolved by declining to answer.
Making the work inspectable

I published CollegeAdvisor-RAG on Hugging Face with architecture notes and usage instructions. A model listing is also available on Kaggle. The portfolio focuses on the retrieval and citation design; benchmark claims in a model card should not be read as a guarantee for every admissions question.
note: The diagram is a simplified presentation of the published architecture. The Hugging Face release is a documented model artifact, not a hosted advisory service.

technical.heading: Retrieval does the factual work.
modules: Search by meaning, rank by authority

Each record is embedded and stored in one of five ChromaDB collections. A question retrieves candidates from every collection, and candidates that cite authoritative domains are boosted before the top results are kept. A minimum score keeps weak matches out of the answer.
Check the question and the source

Specialised handlers route questions about aid, transfer and admissions to the right material. A cite-or-abstain check keeps insufficient evidence visible rather than forcing every question into a confident answer. Student context enters through the application and API.
A smaller model, a narrower job

The published architecture uses a LoRA-adapted TinyLlama 1.1B model for response formatting. The retrieved evidence supplies factual content. Keeping those responsibilities separate makes it easier to inspect whether an answer is supported by its citations.
technical.footnote: Architecture details follow the published model card and my own work on the project. They describe the system’s design, not a guarantee that every retrieved fact is current or every answer is correct.

tour: College advice is full of confident answers with nothing behind them. This assistant works the other way round: find the source first, and if the evidence is thin, say so and stop.
bridge: From answers that must cite a source to a boat that must act on a noisy wind reading: the next island is about deciding under uncertainty in real time.
island: A library with a gate on the way out.
limits: The evaluations were written by the project itself. There is no independent benchmark or real-user accuracy figure.
A citation shows where an answer came from. It does not prove the source is current.
The Hugging Face release is a documented model artifact, not a hosted advisory service.
hotspots: Five collections
Aid policies, major requirements, Common Data Set figures, transfer agreements and worked cited answers, each kept as its own searchable collection.
Cite or abstain
An answer passes only with its sources attached. If the evidence is thin, the card is set aside and the system says why.
Not all sources weigh the same
Official .edu and .gov pages count for more than other material when results are ranked.

title: Language in motion
subtitle: Studying the distance between words and signing.
summary: A language-to-motion research project spanning 3D reconstruction, learned motion codes, and the challenge of evaluating generated signing.
intro: Making science education more accessible led me to a difficult research question: how can language connect to coordinated movement? Sign-Translator explores that question from studio video to a rendered avatar, while keeping generated motion distinct from linguistically validated American Sign Language. No Deaf signer has yet judged its output, and the project says so wherever a result appears.
facts: generated vs. real signing on the project’s back-translation score
Deaf raters so far, by the project’s own count
sections: More than a sequence of hand poses

Signing coordinates the hands, body, face, gaze, and timing. The project represents all of them on one clock: eleven channels at 24 frames per second, covering body and hand rotations, head motion, 52 face coefficients, gaze, blink and contact. Each value carries a mark for whether it was actually observed, so missing data stays visible instead of being silently filled in.
Two cameras, one skeleton

The motion comes from studio video filmed from the front and the side. A pose estimator finds keypoints in each view; the views are synchronised by the motion of the wrists and elbows, the cameras are calibrated from the footage itself, and matching points are triangulated into 3D. One finding from this stage: with both cameras fixed on the signer, focal length cannot be recovered from the geometry alone. Adding a rigid-bone-length term to the calibration brought the focal error from 40–47% to within 1%.
A vocabulary of movement

A residual vector quantiser turns each frame into 32 discrete codes: four body parts (body, left hand, right hand, face) refined through eight stages each. Splitting by part preserves distinctions that a single stream of coordinates would blur, and moving from one codebook to the residual design cut reconstruction error from about 19° and 11 cm to about 8° and 2 cm.
What did not work, and what replaced it

The first plan was to generate a whole sentence of motion from text in one pass. On the project’s instruments, no end-to-end generator separated from blank motion. The current path is composition: generate each word separately, sample it sixteen times, keep the sample a recogniser reads best, and join the words with predicted timing. The output follows English word order, which is not ASL grammar, and the project states this plainly.
Reading the gauge

Generated motion is scored by translating it back to English and comparing with the source sentence, always beside controls: real signing, blank motion, shuffled order and the wrong sentence. On a fresh set of sentences read exactly once, composition scored 2.40, real signing 4.03 and blank motion 2.05. The milestone was 2.55. It was missed, and the result was published without a retry.
note: Active research prototype. The diagrams below document earlier parts of the research design, and the hand image is a rig test. Neither generated movement nor a rendering check establishes linguistically valid ASL. Independent intelligibility evaluation remains necessary. Studio video: How2Sign (CC BY-NC 4.0).

technical.heading: Language has to survive the whole pipeline.
modules: Put the motion on one clock

Front and side How2Sign video are aligned using landmark motion, then the cameras are calibrated, positions triangulated and joint rotations fitted. Reprojection and rigid-bone checks constrain the reconstruction. These are video-derived estimates, with provenance retained, rather than motion-capture ground truth.
Predict codes, not coordinates

An autoregressive transformer predicts the residual codes from text: a causal temporal model over frames, a byte-level text encoder, and a smaller depth model over the eight stages. Early free-running samples were recognised far less often than one-step predictions suggested; trimming, history dropout and masked losses closed most of that gap for isolated words.
Test what the score is measuring

An earlier retrieval evaluator scored motion with zeroed rotations surprisingly well: clip duration was leaking the answer. Fixed two-second windows, randomized offsets, and a duration-only control made that shortcut testable. The same suspicion is applied to every later instrument before it is allowed to grade the generator.
technical.footnote: The release bar was fixed before any human rating: Deaf raters must understand generated sentences at least 70% of the time and within ten points of real signing. That study has been designed but not run. Until it is, nothing here supports a claim of understandable ASL.

tour: Signing uses the hands, face, body and timing together. This project reconstructs that motion in 3D, learns a vocabulary for it, generates it from text, and then asks the hard question: how would you know if it were any good?
bridge: Measuring generated motion honestly sharpens a wider question: what does any single measurement leave out?
island: A capture studio and the instruments that keep it honest.
limits: No Deaf signer has evaluated the generated motion. Automatic scores are a proxy, not comprehension.
The output follows English word order and does not model ASL grammar.
Model weights are not released, and the system is not a deployed translator.

Motion as codes
Each frame becomes 32 small codes: four body parts by eight refinement stages, 24 times a second.
An honest gauge

title: Science, clearly told
subtitle: From a biological idea to a story people can follow.
summary: Website development and entrepreneurship work for an iGEM Gold Medal synthetic biology team.
intro: A scientific project needs a clear explanation of what it does, how it works, and where it might be useful. For LCG-China’s 2024 project on modifying bacterial cellulose, I led the wiki and entrepreneurship work that connected our team’s research with that wider story.
sections: The project behind the pages

The team’s 2024 entry was titled “Modular Bacterial Cellulose Modification Machine in Use and AI Safety Framework in Synthetic Biology.” Bacterial cellulose is a material grown by microbes; the team worked on a modular way to modify it, and paired the laboratory work with a framework for using AI tools safely in synthetic biology.
Giving the research a structure

I directed the team’s website presentation, organizing scientific and business material into accessible explanations of the project, methods, and findings. The wiki gave different parts of the work a shared structure so readers could follow the reasoning as well as the results.
Thinking beyond the laboratory

I led development of the ExploreAid business plan for a proposed bacterial-cellulose bandage. The work considered customer needs, competing products, market positioning, production costs, and commercialization risks.
A team achievement

LCG-China earned an iGEM Gold Medal in 2024. My contribution focused on wiki development, entrepreneurship, and communicating the team’s scientific work to a wider audience. The laboratory and modelling work belongs to my teammates.
note: ExploreAid was a proposed product and business plan; the team medal does not imply clinical validation or commercial release.
tour: Where the route begins: a synthetic-biology team with real results and a judging panel that would meet them through a website. My job was to make the science easy to follow.
bridge: The same year, the question moved from explaining a project to building one people would use every day.
island: A lab on one side, its story on the other.
limits: ExploreAid was a proposed product and business plan. It was not manufactured, tested clinically or sold.
My role was communication and entrepreneurship. I did not lead the laboratory or computational work.
A team medal reflects the whole team’s project against iGEM’s criteria, not an individual result.

title: Finding a heading
subtitle: Software that has to answer to the wind.
summary: Control and simulation improvements for an autonomous sailboat navigating changing conditions.
intro: An autonomous boat has to turn imperfect information into a physical decision. My contributions to Kehillah Sailbot focused on navigation, steering, wind filtering, state estimation, and the simulator used to study the boat’s behavior. The little boat that carries you between the islands on this site’s front page is modelled on the team’s simulated trimaran.
facts: best upwind angle in the team’s polar table
rudder travel the controller must respect
quantities tracked by the state estimator
sections: Closing the loop

The team’s system runs on ROS 2: sensors publish GPS fixes, wind direction and inertial readings; a navigation node decides; rudder and sail commands leave on their own topics. I contributed to the software between those ends: smoothing the wind reading and flagging gusts, estimating the boat’s state, and turning a desired heading into commands.
Where to point, given the wind

A sailboat cannot sail straight into the wind. The team’s planner reads a polar table of boat speed against wind angle and uses its best angles (49.3° off the wind going upwind, 124.4° going downwind) to decide when a course needs a tack and where the turn should happen. The baseline sail trim is a simple proportional rule, and the boat on this site’s front page uses the same one.
Respecting physical constraints

My model-predictive steering work predicts the boat’s heading a few steps ahead with a first-order yaw model and chooses rudder moves that keep the heading error, the turn rate and the rudder effort small. The rudder’s ±21° travel and its maximum rate are hard constraints, and heel beyond 25° is penalised. The model’s constants are assumed defaults, not values calibrated on the water.
Estimating what cannot be measured directly

A square-root unscented Kalman filter tracks ten quantities, including position, heading, speeds, heel and both actuator angles, from GPS, compass and inertial measurements. A separate sail optimiser uses lift and drag relations, including a post-stall model, to suggest trim and to ease the sail as heel builds.
Learning in simulation

The team’s physics simulator models a 15 kg trimaran on a small lake, with lift and drag on the sail and hulls taken from published coefficient tables. My work there was engineering hardening: input validation, error handling, logging and typed constants, so that a wrong configuration fails loudly instead of producing a plausible-looking run. Nothing in this page is an on-water result.
note: The island is an illustration. This page describes software contributions and does not report unverified competition or on-water performance.

technical.heading: A decision becomes a rudder angle.
modules: Connect the control loop

The team’s ROS 2 architecture separates sensor input, navigation, and actuation. GPS fixes and wind direction feed the control system, while rudder and sail commands travel on dedicated topics. That separation makes the data entering a decision and the command leaving it inspectable.
Constrain the next move

The steering controller minimises a cost over a ten-step horizon: heading error, yaw rate and change in rudder angle, with a terminal heading term. It is solved under a rudder limit of ±21° and a slew limit of 15° per second, so the plan only contains moves the servo can make. If the optimiser fails, the proportional controller remains as the fallback.
Study behavior before deployment

The simulator integrates forces of the form ½·C·ρ·v²·A on each foil with several sub-steps per time step. It connects the software question (what command should be issued?) with the physical question of how the boat responds. Parameters in the controller and the simulator do not yet agree with each other, and reconciling them is open work.

title: A better test for an agent
subtitle: Making software experiments easier to trust.
summary: Repository-task evaluation and training-data tools for studying a coding agent’s behavior.
intro: Before asking whether a coding agent improved, it helps to know exactly what it was tested on. This project builds the infrastructure behind that question for a repository-repair agent based on Gemma 4: task provenance, evaluation isolation, deterministic training schedules, and recoverable runs. Its working rule is that no claim should rest on an unverified step.
facts: tools the agent is allowed to use
gates before a training example is admitted
public tasks screened and frozen into splits
tasks in the first admitted training set
sections: The job being tested

The agent is given a real open-source repository and a reported issue. It may use exactly nine tools, covering running commands, reading and editing files, checking status, navigating code structure and submitting a patch. Whether the patch is correct is decided by tests it never sees.
A sealed room and two kinds of test

Each task runs in a container with the network switched off. A valid task must fail before the fix and pass after it: the tests that were failing must now pass, and the tests that were passing must still pass. Parsers for five test frameworks read the per-case results and reject summaries whose totals contradict their own cases.
Knowing where each task came from

From 32,079 candidate rows, 4,818 were eligible and 2,966 were selected and frozen into training, development and confirmation splits, separated by repository and by owner so the same project cannot appear on both sides. Licence files were checked at each task’s pinned commit, which caught four repositories carrying copyleft text under a permissive label.
Four gates and two checkers

Training examples begin in quarantine. They are admitted only through four gates: rights and attribution, split isolation, runtime qualification, and task alignment. A separate audit module then recomputes every quantity without sharing code with the loader, so the two must agree independently. The first admitted set holds 51 tasks.
Separating infrastructure from performance

The model is a 4-bit Gemma 4 with a small LoRA adapter. So far it has taken one update on a tiny fixture; the first real training step ran out of memory, was diagnosed, and was fixed in code that has not yet been re-measured on a GPU. No sustained training has run, so the project does not claim that the agent has learned anything yet.
note: Research tooling in development. The project does not yet establish learned performance gains on unseen repository tasks.

technical.heading: Make an improvement reproducible.
modules: Track the task’s lineage

Repository tasks carry source provenance and evaluation contracts. Checks for overlap and quarantine keep questionable material out of the training path. This makes the boundary between development data and held-out evaluation something the tooling can inspect.
Read the tests, not just the headline

The test audit preserves individual case outcomes and rejects contradictory aggregate counts. Failures, errors, and skipped cases remain distinct. A successful process exit or an attractive summary count cannot substitute for the underlying test evidence.
Translate actions, replay results

Teacher trajectories from another agent framework are converted to the nine-tool format under a fixed set of rules. Tool results are deliberately not translated: they must come from replaying the action, because rewriting them would fabricate runtime output. One untranslatable call rejects the whole trajectory.
technical.footnote: These are implemented evaluation and training-preparation mechanisms. The repository does not yet establish learned gains on unseen repository tasks, and this page makes no claim about a competition result.
